description: A remote technology and blockchain development team founded in 2025, bringing together expertise in full-stack engineering, Web3 technologies, Solana development, and smart contract systems. We build practical, innovative software solutions and enjoy applying our technical skills to real-world challenges. For NASA Space Apps Challenge, our team aims to combine software engineering, creativity, and data-driven problem-solving to develop accessible solutions using NASA’s open data.
summary:
MISSION VIGIL is a 3D browser game. Students wake up alone in a sleeping Mars base and have to keep it alive. It isn't a dashboard to click through. You walk an astronaut around the outpost and do every job by hand: you fix the air, share out the power, grow food and hide from a solar flare. ARIA, a small flying helper robot, guides you and tells the story.

Chapter 1, "Cold Start", lasts five sols (days on Mars), and each sol adds one new demand on top of the last. That's the heart of the challenge. There is only so much power. Whatever you give the heater can't run the air cleaner or make oxygen, so every choice costs something, and players feel it for themselves.

The science is real. The oxygen and CO₂ numbers come from NASA technical reports. The weather station shows 30 sols of real data from the Curiosity rover, and a live map uses NASA JPL orbit data to show how long a radio message takes to reach Earth today. The game has 25 "Did you know?" cards, each with its source, and we clearly mark which numbers we tuned for gameplay.

It runs in any web browser with nothing to install and no account. It works with a keyboard or touch, and it's written for kids. We made it because we believe the web can teach best when children step inside the lesson, not just read about it.
details:
What it does

MISSION VIGIL: Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer is a 3D game that runs in a web browser. You play an astronaut who wakes up alone in a Mars base that has gone to sleep. The air is slowly going bad, and the only way to fix things is to walk over and do the work yourself. You put a new filter in the air cleaner and share out power at the power box. You put on a spacesuit to clean dust off the solar panels. You water the salad, patch a leak, and stack bags into a shelter when a solar flare hits.

Chapter 1, "Cold Start", lasts five sols (days on Mars). Each sol adds one new demand: air, then power and heat, then food and water, then radiation, then the call home. The earlier jobs don't go away, so by the last sol you're keeping everything going at once. That's the challenge brief turned into play: one decision affects all the others. Power is limited, and the air cleaner, the oxygen maker and the heater all share it. Put it all into oxygen and the CO₂ climbs. Forget the heater at night and the base freezes.

How it teaches

ARIA, a small flying helper robot, tells the story and teaches one control at a time. A yellow trail on the floor always leads to the next must-do job. Blue jobs are optional. They pay parts for the 3D printer and unlock "Did you know?" cards. There are 25 cards, and each links what you just did to something that really happened, with its source. One covers the square filter the Apollo 13 crew fitted into a round hole. Another covers the InSight lander, whose mission ended when dust covered its solar panels. Another covers MOXIE, which made oxygen from Mars air. When you fail, the screen tells you what happened, what to try next, and the true story behind it. A "?" button answers the big questions at any time.

Real NASA data

  • The oxygen, CO₂, food and water a person needs each day come from NASA technical reports.
  • The weather station shows 30 sols of real temperature and pressure readings from the Curiosity rover.
  • A live map uses NASA JPL orbit data to show where Earth and Mars are today, and how long a radio message takes between them.

We keep real numbers apart from the ones we tuned for gameplay. Every value in the code is tagged "real" or "game", and every source is listed in our SOURCES.md file.

Tools we used

We wrote it in TypeScript with Next.js, React, Three.js (through React Three Fiber), Zustand and Tailwind CSS, and it's hosted on Vercel. The game uses no image, 3D model or sound files. The base is built from simple shapes in code, the icons are drawn by hand as SVG, and every sound is made live with the Web Audio API. The simulation is plain TypeScript with its own tests, kept apart from the graphics.

What we thought about

  • Kids are the players. We use short sentences and everyday words, like "air cleaner" instead of "CO₂ scrubber". Every number comes with what it means.
  • Everyone can play. It works with taps on a phone or with the keyboard alone. Screen readers can read the gauges, and the game respects the setting for reduced motion.
  • School computers. There's nothing to install, no account and no tracking. The 3D scene loads after the page. In our tests it held 60 frames per second even with the processor slowed to a quarter of its speed.
  • Being honest about the science. Some things are sped up so the game is playable. A sol takes 100 seconds, and the solar flare is much stronger than a real one would feel on Mars. The game says so, and doesn't present these as facts.
  • Reasons to play again. There are stars, ranks, 6 badges, 5 hidden secrets, a best score, a postcard from Mars to save, and a certificate to print.

Why it matters

Reading that people breathe out CO₂ is one thing. Watching it rise in your own base, and fixing it before it's too late, is another. We want students to come away knowing why air, power, food and shelter all depend on each other, and that real crews face these same trade-offs. Chapter 1 is the first of six planned chapters, which go from a sleeping base on Mars to splashdown on Earth. More broadly, it shows that one web page can hold a living 3D world, a working simulation and real NASA data, and we think that approach could teach many other subjects too.
